aiOverview.content: The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified on August 18, 1920, prohibited denying citizens the right to vote based on sex, effectively granting women nationwide suffrage. Following decades of advocacy by activists like Susan B. Anthony and Alice Paul, Tennessee provided the final necessary vote for ratification. Key Aspects of the 19th Amendment: Ratification & Adoption: Ratified on August 18, 1920, it was formally certified on August 26, 1920, by Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby, as described in this article from the US House of Representatives. Purpose: The amendment ensures that "[t]he right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex". The Struggle: The victory was secured after nearly a century of marches, protests, and lobbying, gaining momentum during World War I. Limitations: Despite the amendment, many women of color—particularly African Americans, Native Americans, and Asian Americans—remained disenfranchised by state-level voter suppression, such as poll taxes and literacy tests, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965, notes this article from the City of West Hollywood. Key Figures and Organizations: Leaders: Key advocates included Ida B. Wells, Alice Paul, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott, and Susan B. Anthony. Organizations: The National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) played a key role in organizing the movement, according to this video from the YouTube channel "Journey to American Democracy". Impact: It immediately enfranchised 26 million American women in time for the 1920 presidential election, as explained in this video from the YouTube channel "Journey to American Democracy". It legally validated women's right to participate in local, state, and national elections.
